title: Greetings & polite phrases
sub: Say hello, goodbye and ask how someone is.
subject: Greetings & polite phrases

boards.say: Every match starts with a handshake. In German, every conversation starts with a greeting. Learn these first and you can walk onto the pitch.
pts: Pick the greeting by the time of day

boards.say: Four greetings, one for each part of the day. Tap a word to hear it.
Two ways to leave the pitch. Informal with friends, formal with strangers and teachers.
Think of two formations. Friends play the informal system, strangers the formal one. Same question, different shape.
Pick an answer from the scale, from best to worst.
Listen first, then read. Tap Play and hear both players.
Now the formal version, as with a teacher.
lines: Guten Tag. Wie geht es Ihnen?

boards.q: A stranger, a teacher: which goodbye fits?
boards.why: Auf Wiedersehen is the formal goodbye. Tschüs is for friends.

boards.q: It is 9 in the morning. What do you say?
boards.why: Morgen = morning. Gute Nacht is only when going to bed.

boards.say: Final whistle! You can start and end any conversation. Train these words now so they stick.
boards.subject: Greetings & polite phrases

title: Classroom & instructions
sub: Understand your teacher and ask for help.
subject: Classroom & instructions

boards.say: Before the real game, the coach shouts instructions. In class your teacher does the same. Learn to understand them and you never get lost.
pts: The verb comes first, like a whistle

boards.say: These verbs are the basic training skills.
Your teacher gives orders. Each one starts with the verb and ends with Sie.
When you are stuck, use these. A good player always asks.
An instruction is short: the verb leads, Sie follows. Add a small word at the end if needed.
A normal minute in the classroom.

boards.q: Your teacher says: Hören Sie noch einmal. What do you do?
boards.why: hören = to listen, noch einmal = once more.

boards.q: You did not understand. What do you say?
boards.why: Wie bitte? means Pardon? Ask when you did not catch it.

boards.say: Training complete. You can follow every instruction in class. Now practise the words.
boards.subject: Classroom & instructions

title: Sounds & articles
sub: German spelling sounds, and the three little words der, die, das.

boards.say: German is easier than it looks, because it is spelled as it sounds. A few sound rules and you can read any word.
Learn these sound patterns. Each one has an example from your notes.
Two more tricks that German players use all the time.
Tap each word and say it back out loud.
Every German noun wears a shirt: der, die or das. This is the gender. There are no tricks to guess it, so always learn the noun with its article.
Same word 'the', four shirts.

boards.why: das Kind. Always learn the article with the noun.
die: die Eltern, die Kinder. All plurals use die.

boards.say: You can now pronounce German and you know the three articles. Next time you meet a noun, grab its article too.

title: Introductions & names
sub: Say who you are and ask who someone is.
subject: Introductions & names

boards.say: Every player gives his name before kick-off. Here is how you introduce yourself, and the two key verbs: sein and heißen.
pts: Ich heiße ... / Ich bin ... / Mein Name ist ...

boards.say: Three ways to say who you are. They mean the same.
Same question, informal and formal. Remember: du for friends, Sie for strangers.
The most important verb in the squad. It is irregular, so learn it by heart.
Regular, with one trick: the stem ends in ß, so du only gets -t.
Two new teammates meet.
lines: My name is Sina. And you?

boards.say: At the front desk.
lines: Good day. What is your name?

boards.why: du heißt. With du the verb ends in -t.
ich bin. Learn the sein line-up: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind.

boards.say: Now everyone knows who you are. Train this subject to lock it in.
boards.subject: Introductions & names

title: Numbers
sub: Count from 0 to 100 and build any number in between.
subject: Numbers

boards.say: Football is numbers: scores, shirt numbers, minutes. Count 0 to 12 by heart, then German builds the rest with simple patterns.
The first twelve. No pattern, just learn them.
Easy pattern: unit + zehn.
Add -zig. Watch for the three rule-breakers.
Three tens bend the pattern. Dreißig uses ß instead of -zig. Sechzig drops the s of sechs. Siebzig drops the en of sieben.
For 21 to 99 German says the unit FIRST, then und, then the tens. Like a scoreline read backwards.
Say them out loud.

boards.why: Unit first: acht + und + zwanzig = 28.
sechzehn = sechs without the s + zehn. Sechzig is 60.

boards.say: You can read any scoreboard now. Train the numbers to get fast.
boards.subject: Numbers

title: Everyday verbs
sub: Make regular verbs work with every player, plus haben.
subject: Everyday verbs

boards.say: Verbs are your players. They change their ending depending on who is playing. Learn one pattern and most verbs follow it.
These will work in almost every conversation.
Take the stem, add the ending. kommen → komm- + ending.
See the endings at work.
haben is irregular. Careful: er/sie/es is hat, not habt.
When the stem ends in t, add an extra e so you can say it. arbeiten = to work.

boards.h: Match tape: getting to know you
boards.say: A short chat using the new verbs.

boards.why: du hast. Ich habe, du hast, er hat.
With du the ending is -st: du kommst.

boards.say: Now you can talk about what people do. Train the verbs next.
boards.subject: Everyday verbs

title: Questions
sub: Ask anything with W-questions and yes/no questions.
subject: Questions & answers

boards.say: A question is a set piece. There are only two types, and each has a fixed shape. Learn the shape and you can ask anything.
pts: W-Frage: starts with a question word

boards.say: All W-questions start with W. Learn them as a group.
Question word first. The verb is always player number 2.
No question word. The verb jumps to position 1 and the answer is ja or nein.
A short interview with questions of both types.
lines: How many books do you have?

boards.q: Put the words in order: Where do you live?
boards.why: W-word first, then the verb in position 2, then the subject.
It starts with the verb, so the answer is ja or nein.

boards.q: Where is the verb in a W-Frage?
boards.why: Always position 2: Wo wohnst du?

boards.say: You can now ask any question in the match. Train these question words.
boards.subject: Questions & answers

title: Personal details
sub: Age, family status, children and the words on a form.
subject: Personal details

boards.say: A player card lists age, status and where he plays. A German form asks the same things. Here is the vocabulary.
Three questions, three groups of people.
The word for the status box on the form is Familienstand.
Together or alone? With children?
Learn these to fill in an application.
Fill in the player card out loud.
lines: Ich wohne in Hamburg. Ich lebe allein.
I live in Hamburg. I live alone.

boards.why: ledig = single. geschieden = divorced, verlobt = engaged.

boards.q: Which is the form field for your job?
boards.why: Beruf = profession. Wohnort is your place of residence.

boards.say: Your player card is ready. Train the personal details.
boards.subject: Personal details

title: Countries
sub: Say where you come from and where you live: aus and in.
subject: Countries & languages

boards.say: Where do you come from, and where do you play now? German uses two small words for that: aus for the origin, in for the present place.
Most countries have no article.
These wear a shirt. After aus it changes: die → der, der → dem, plural → den.
Use aus with the origin. For countries with an article, take care of the shirt.
Use in for the current place.
Two players from different countries chat.
lines: Ich komme aus der Türkei. Und Sie?
I come from Turkey. And you?

boards.why: aus = origin. in is for where you live now.
die Schweiz → aus der Schweiz.

boards.say: Passport checked. Train the countries now.
boards.subject: Countries & languages

title: Jobs & work
sub: Ask and tell what you do, and make the feminine form.
subject: Jobs & work

boards.say: Even players have another job. Learn to say what you do for a living, and how male and female job titles work.
The female form usually adds -in. Sometimes an umlaut appears too.
Same -in pattern.
Male job + -in = female job. Student → Studentin. Kellner → Kellnerin. Arzt → Ärztin (with an umlaut).
Two questions, three ways to answer.
als = the role. bei = the employer.
Not working yet? Say it like this.
Talking about jobs.
lines: What do you do for a living?
I am a waitress. And you?

boards.q: Which is the female form of der Student?
boards.why: Add -in: die Studentin.
bei HotSped = at HotSped. als is the role.

boards.say: Your career is clear. Train the job vocabulary.
boards.subject: Jobs & work

title: Family
sub: Name your family members and say mein / meine.
subject: Family

boards.say: Every player has a family in the stands. Learn the family words, and the two small words mein and meine.
Informal words in a second line.
The close family.
Uncles, aunts and partners.
mein for der and das. meine for die and every plural. dein works the same way.
To say whose it is, add -s to the name. No apostrophe.
Looking at family photos.
lines: Nein, das ist mein Onkel Otto.
No, that is my uncle Otto.
Und das? Ist das deine Oma?
And that? Is that your grandma?

boards.why: die Schwester → meine Schwester.
der Vater → mein Vater.

boards.say: The family is in the stands. Train the family words.
boards.subject: Family

boards.say: With a normal question you say ja or nein. With a negative question German has a special word: doch. Think of it as a VAR override: the question says no, the truth is yes.
No nicht in the question. Ja means yes, nein means no.
The question has nicht, kein or oder? at the end. Doch means: yes, it IS so. Nein means: no, it is NOT so.
rows: Wohnen deine Eltern nicht in Hamburg?
Wohnen deine Eltern nicht in Hamburg?

boards.say: Doch only answers a negative question and always means yes. Think: doch = 'on the contrary, yes'.
Ja, nein and doch in one chat.
lines: Wohnen deine Eltern nicht in Hamburg?
Don't your parents live in Hamburg?
Do Georg and Angela live together?

boards.q: Ist Maren nicht geschieden? She IS divorced. Answer:
boards.why: A negative question and the answer is yes: Doch.

boards.q: Ist das dein Bruder? He is NOT your brother. Answer:
boards.why: A positive question and the answer is no: Nein.

boards.say: VAR approved. Train the questions and answers.
boards.subject: Questions & answers

title: Noun genders
sub: Rules to guess der, die or das from the word.
subject: Noun genders

boards.say: Most nouns have no logic. But many follow rules by ending or by category. These rules guess most of the squad correctly.
Alcohol, car brands, times and weather are usually der.
rows: der Gin, der Wodka (exception: das Bier)
der BMW, der Honda (exception: das Auto)
der Tag, der Monat, der Januar, der Mittwoch, der Frühling

boards.say: These endings are almost always die.
These are das.

Every rule has exceptions. Times: die Woche, die Nacht, das Jahr. Weather: das Gewitter, die Sonne. Nouns in -e: der Name, der Buchstabe, das Auge, das Ende. -o: die Disko. Ge-: die Gesundheit, die Gebühr.

boards.why: -eit is always die: die Krankheit.
-chen is always das, even for a girl: das Mädchen.
Alcohol is usually der: der Wodka.

boards.say: You can guess most genders now. Train them for real.
boards.subject: Noun genders

title: Furniture & home
sub: Name the things in your home and the shop.
subject: Furniture & home

boards.say: Look around the dressing room: table, chairs, lamp. These are the home words. Remember: learn each one with its article.
Tap each and look at its shirt.
On the wall and in the room.
Name things in the room.

boards.why: der Stuhl.
die Lampe: nouns in -e are mostly die.

boards.say: The dressing room is furnished. Train the furniture words.
boards.subject: Furniture & home

title: Describing & prices
sub: Adjectives, opinions, and asking the price.
subject: Describing & prices

boards.say: At the transfer market you describe the player and ask the price. In a shop it is the same: adjectives, opinion and price.
Learn them in pairs.
A thing is replaced by the pronoun that matches its article.
Wie findest du ...? asks what you think. Ich finde ... gives your opinion.
items: what do you think of the picture?
Ich finde, das Bild ist teuer.
I think the picture is expensive.

boards.say: Prices in euros.
The whole shopping conversation.
lines: Wir sind im Möbelgeschäft. Wie findest du das Bild?
We are in the furniture shop. What do you think of the picture?
Ich finde, das Bild ist teuer.
I think the picture is expensive.
Das finde ich auch. Der Stuhl ist schön.
I agree. The chair is beautiful.
Oh, das ist aber günstig! Das ist ein Sonderangebot.
Oh, that is really cheap! That is a special offer.

boards.why: die → sie: Die Lampe ist schön. Sie ist schön.

boards.q: What is the opposite of teuer?
boards.why: teuer ↔ günstig / billig.

boards.say: Deal signed. Train the describing words.
boards.subject: Describing & prices

title: Verbs with vowel change
sub: Verbs that change their vowel with du and er/sie/es.
subject: Verbs with vowel change

boards.say: Some verbs swap their vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms. The other forms stay normal. Think of it as a player changing position in the middle.
Only du and er/sie/es change.
nehmen also doubles the m: nimmst, nimmt.
lesen and sehen change to ie.
a becomes ä.
Learn them with their changing forms.
See them in action.
items: You sleep for a long time.

boards.why: sprechen: du sprichst.
schlafen: er schläft (a → ä).

boards.say: You have the full tactics board. Train the changing verbs.
boards.subject: Verbs with vowel change

title: Languages
sub: Say which languages you speak and how well.
subject: Countries & languages

boards.say: The last match of the season: languages. You can already say where you are from. Now say what you speak and how well.
Language = country + -isch (mostly).
From best to worst.
Verb in position 2 again. Sprechen changes its vowel with du: du sprichst.
Two players, many languages.
lines: Ich spreche sehr gut Deutsch und ein bisschen Türkisch.
I speak German very well and a little Turkish.
Yes. And I am learning German.
I do not speak Chinese at all.

boards.q: How do you say: I speak a little German?
boards.why: ein bisschen = a little bit.
du sprichst: e → i.

boards.say: Champions! You have covered every lesson in the notes. Train the languages and keep the streak.
boards.subject: Countries & languages
